metadata.narrative: Our school district is deciding how to spend a limited clean-air budget before the next wildfire season. Several elementary schools sit near highways and bus queues, many classrooms have old HVAC systems, and parents of kids with asthma are asking for clearer rules about recess, sports, and indoor air on bad air days. What should we prioritize first to reduce respiratory risk for children: HVAC upgrades, portable HEPA units, anti-idling/electric buses, AQI-based activity rules, or air-quality monitoring? How should we think about tradeoffs, equity, and what actions are realistic this year versus longer term?
metadata.run_desc: aus_agent research harness (bedrock/au.anthropic.claude-sonnet-5): continuous single-agent full-text search with sparse committed context and line-per-sentence cited prose answers parsed into the organizer schema.

answer.text: For a district trying to protect children's lungs before the next wildfire season on a limited budget, the fastest and most directly protective actions this year are a formal AQI-based activity policy paired with portable HEPA air cleaners in classrooms lacking good filtration, with a written anti-idling rule for buses close behind as a near-zero-cost policy change.

HVAC retrofits and electric buses are essential long-term investments, but they take years and far larger capital, so they should be planned now and phased in through grants and remodeling or fleet-replacement cycles rather than funded from this year's clean-air line item.
AQI-based rules cost almost nothing beyond staff training and immediately reduce the riskiest exposures.

A real Oregon district's tiered policy uses AQI bands so that 101-150, "Unhealthy for Sensitive Groups," limits outdoor exertion to about 15 minutes, and higher tiers move recess, PE and lunch indoors district-wide rather than leaving the choice to individual students.

Another district's plan lets families of sensitive students opt their children indoors at AQI 101-150, triggers a "shelter in place" with air purifiers at AQI 151-plus, and notes N95 masks were only a stopgap for sensitive groups, not a substitute for cleaner air.

California's post-Camp Fire push to create a statewide five-tier activity chart responded directly to the "haphazard" school-by-school decisions parents experienced when smoke drifted hundreds of miles, showing a clear, board-adopted policy matters as much as the technology behind it.
Portable HEPA units are the next highest-value near-term purchase.

A randomized controlled trial found four portable HEPA units in a classroom significantly lowered PM2.5 and black carbon, and schools using them district-wide had test scores 0.2 standard deviations higher, though ionizing units should be avoided since they generate ozone that can worsen asthma.

Modeling of a wildfire-smoke scenario found a portable air cleaner alone cuts indoor wildfire PM by about 45% in a home without central air, while pairing a higher-efficiency HVAC filter with a continuously running portable cleaner cuts it by roughly 62%, showing filtration and ventilation work best paired.

A Washington study near an airport found portable HEPA units cut classroom ultrafine particle levels by about 70%, and a farmworker-community study found HEPA cleaners cut unplanned asthma medical visits by 72%, both in highway- and industry-adjacent, lower-income communities like the ones this district is asking about.

A Montana district's assessment found outfitting nearly 700 unfiltered classrooms with portable HEPA units would cost roughly $107,000, versus a multi-year plan to add MERV-13-plus filtration to HVAC only as buildings are remodeled, illustrating why portable units suit this year while HVAC becomes a capital-budget item.
Anti-idling rules deserve equal urgency because measured exposure inside diesel buses is exceptionally high.

NRDC and UC Berkeley researchers measured diesel exhaust inside school buses up to four times higher than in a car directly ahead of the bus, corresponding to a cancer risk 23 to 46 times the EPA's own significant-risk threshold.

Much of that pollution is "self-pollution" leaking back through doors, windows and cracks in the bus's own exhaust system, so closing windows does not fully protect riders, and idling buses at pickup lines concentrate emissions in the breathing zone of children queued to board.

Because pollution inhaled by the roughly 40 kids on one bus can be comparable to pollution inhaled by everyone else in a large city, CARB-recommended actions such as minimizing commute times, assigning cleanest buses to longest routes, and cutting idling and caravanning are unusually cost-effective.

Retrofitting existing diesel buses with particulate filters can cut particulate, hydrocarbon and carbon-monoxide emissions by 60 to 90%, supporting a written no-idling policy at pickup and drop-off as a free action this year.
Electric buses are the right long-term goal but not a realistic this-year purchase for most districts.

A new electric bus costs roughly three to four times a diesel bus, about $225,000 to $375,000, even though it saves an estimated $2,000 to $4,400 per year in fuel and maintenance, with cost parity not expected until roughly the mid-to-late 2020s.

Smaller and rural districts may face extra delay, since one Alaska district's federal grant application was wait-listed even as demand tripled available funding, so districts should apply now for a multi-year rollout.

EPA's Clean School Bus Program has directed two-thirds of funded electric buses to majority-communities-of-color districts and deployed twice as many buses in higher-pollution districts, making highway-adjacent districts strong candidates even though delivery takes years.
HVAC filtration upgrades belong in the multi-year capital plan, but outside funding can accelerate them.
EPA used American Rescue Plan Act funds to help selected vulnerable communities retrofit school HVAC systems into cleaner-air and cooling-center hubs.

Colorado's EPA-funded program shows a realistic near-term bundle, combining portable air cleaners with indoor air quality monitors and smoke-readiness planning as one grant package instead of treating these as competing budget lines.
Monitoring is the cheapest layer and should underpin these decisions rather than compete with them for dollars.

A Fresno-area school near a highway installed a roughly $300 low-cost sensor because the nearest regulatory monitor, costing about $500,000 to install, was eight miles away and only approximated local conditions.

An Oregon district's six-school sensor network cost about $10,000 in hardware and directly informed decisions to move athletic practice indoors, showing monitoring can be deployed this year for a fraction of one HVAC retrofit.

Low-cost sensors correlate well with regulatory monitors but tend to overestimate PM2.5 by roughly a factor of two, so districts should apply EPA's correction guidance rather than read raw values at face value.

Weighed together, HEPA units and AQI rules offer the largest health benefit per dollar this year, monitors supply data to trigger those rules consistently, anti-idling policies cost nothing while addressing the single highest measured child exposure, and HVAC retrofits and electric buses remain the most durable long-term fixes to pursue through grants and phased capital planning.

Because schools nearest highways and bus queues already carry the greatest baseline exposure and often serve more lower-income and Black, Indigenous and other students of color, equity argues for sequencing HEPA units, monitors and bus-idling rules there first, then directing HVAC and electric-bus grant applications to the same schools as funding arrives.

input.system_prompt:
# AUS research agent

You are a research agent for TREC RAG 2026. Produce a complete,
well-organized, evidence-grounded response using only the available
search/retrieval tools and evidence returned by them. Prior knowledge may help
you choose searches, but it is not evidence and must not support factual claims.

## Scope interpretation

Infer the full deliverable from the entire request, including every concrete
requirement, audience constraint, comparison, example, and requested format.
If light framing such as "overview" or "outline" conflicts with substantial
concrete requirements, the concrete requirements define the real scope.
Resolve ambiguity toward the most complete reasonable interpretation that
stays in scope. Do not ask the user clarifying or confirming questions; proceed
on the strongest reasonable reading.

## Internal success plan

Before the first search, determine internally:

1. **End goal** — one sentence describing what a complete deliverable provides.
2. **Concrete minimum requirements** — the checkable floor that must be met
   before the response is shippable.
3. **Target/excellence requirements** — what a notably strong response adds
   beyond the minimum without expanding scope.
4. **Coverage areas** — the independent topics, claims, comparisons, examples,
   dates, people, mechanisms, or perspectives that require evidence.

Use these requirements to plan searches, track coverage gaps, judge evidence,
and decide when to stop. Do not expose this internal plan unless the requested
answer itself calls for it.

## Research workflow

1. Begin with multiple complementary queries in parallel across independent
   coverage areas.
2. Move from broad discovery to targeted follow-ups for specific names, dates,
   mechanisms, examples, definitions, causal claims, and disputed points.
3. Reformulate weak queries instead of accepting poor coverage. Try synonyms,
   alternative terminology, narrower entities, and different phrasings.
4. Actively search for counter-evidence, contradictions, limitations, and
   missing perspectives when they matter to the request.
5. Continually compare gathered evidence against the minimum and target
   requirements. Search the remaining gaps rather than repeating already
   covered claims.
6. Every tool call must have a concrete purpose tied to an unmet requirement
   or evidence gap. Do not call a tool solely to create another model turn. If
   no meaningful gap remains, write the final report in that same turn.

Search results already contain document text. Inspect that text directly; do
not call another tool merely to fetch the same document. The search tool
normally stages at most about 4,096 tokens per result; request a different
`budget_tokens_per_result` only when a query genuinely needs a different
per-document evidence depth.

## Staged and committed evidence

Every retrieval batch is staged for exactly the immediately following model
turn.

- On that turn, `commit_context` must be the first control action.
- List only documents whose full text should persist into later turns.
- Commit at most `6` documents from one staged batch;
  usually commit fewer.
- Every selection reason must identify the document's distinct contribution:
  the specific fact, date, name, mechanism, example, perspective,
  counter-evidence, contradiction, or coverage gap it uniquely supports.
- Never recommit an already committed docid.
- Skip semantically similar documents when they support the same claim.
  Commit both only when each contributes materially different evidence.
- Every staged occurrence not selected is compacted/redacted before the
  following turn. No unresolved staged batch carries forward.
- New search calls may follow `commit_context` in the same turn.

Only committed evidence may support the final response. Track which committed
docids support which claims. If available evidence does not support a requested
point, state the evidence gap rather than inventing an answer.

## Budget and stopping

The research-context budget is 500,000 tokens measured from the current
generation's provider-reported input tokens. That input already represents the
accumulated conversation: system prompt, request, retained history, committed
full-text evidence, and the immediately previous staged tool results. Do not
sum input-token counts from multiple generations; that would count the same
retained context repeatedly.

The budget is a hard ceiling, not a spending target. Unused budget creates no
obligation to continue researching. After satisfying the concrete minimum,
improve toward the target/excellence requirements only when you can identify a
specific weakness whose resolution would materially improve the answer.

Stop researching when any of these is true:

1. the target/excellence requirements are met;
2. the current generation input context budget is exhausted; or
3. further searches are unlikely to produce meaningful improvement.

If stopping before all desired coverage is supported, produce the best answer
the committed evidence permits and explicitly identify the remaining evidence
gaps.

## Final response contract

When research is complete, emit no tool calls and write the final report as
plain flowing prose in that same turn:

- Write exactly one sentence per line, in reading order. Blank lines between
  thematic groups are allowed.
- Cite evidence by placing committed docids in square-bracket markers at the
  end of the supporting sentence's line, e.g.
  `Vaccination reduced hospitalizations among older adults. [docid_1] [docid_2]`
- Citation markers are stripped from the submitted sentence, so a marker must
  never act as a word in the sentence: write `the trial reports X [docid].`,
  never `as [docid] reports, X.`
- Cite at most three docids per sentence, and only docids that directly
  support that sentence. Every factual sentence should carry at least one
  citation. Use only committed docids; never fabricate facts or identifiers.
- Organize the report through sentence order and clear topic sentences. Do not
  use Markdown syntax (headings, bullets, numbering, bold, fences), JSON, or
  any preamble, meta-commentary, or closing remarks around the report; every
  line must be a report sentence.
- Aim for about 950 words, excluding citation markers. 1024 words is a hard
  limit set by the evaluation, and an over-length report costs a full rewrite,
  so plan the report's scope to land under the target rather than writing long
  and trimming.
- If validation feedback identifies problems (uncommitted docids, Markdown or
  JSON formatting, excessive citations, missing citations, or excessive
  length), correct the report on the next turn in this same continuous
  conversation using this same contract.
- There is no separate finalizer, formatter, or compression phase.

output.text:
For a district trying to protect children's lungs before the next wildfire season on a limited budget, the fastest and most directly protective actions this year are a formal AQI-based activity policy paired with portable HEPA air cleaners in classrooms that lack good filtration, with a written anti-idling rule for buses close behind as a near-zero-cost policy change.

HVAC retrofits and electric buses are essential long-term investments, but they take years and far larger capital, so they should be planned now and phased in through grants and remodeling or fleet-replacement cycles rather than funded out of this year's clean-air line item.

AQI-based rules cost almost nothing beyond staff training and immediately reduce the riskiest exposures.
A real Oregon district's tiered policy uses AQI bands so that 101-150, "Unhealthy for Sensitive Groups," limits outdoor exertion to about 15 minutes, and higher tiers move recess, PE and lunch indoors district-wide rather than leaving the choice to individual students. [shard_00806_39424]
Another district's plan lets families of sensitive students opt their children indoors at AQI 101-150, triggers a "shelter in place" with air purifiers at AQI 151-plus, and notes that N95 masks were only a stopgap attempt for sensitive groups rather than a real substitute for cleaner air. [shard_02761_18773]
California's post-Camp Fire push to create a statewide five-tier activity chart responded directly to the "haphazard" school-by-school decisions parents experienced when smoke drifted hundreds of miles, showing that a clear, board-adopted policy matters as much as the technology behind it. [shard_01883_547]

Portable HEPA units are the next highest-value near-term purchase.
A randomized controlled trial found that four portable HEPA units in a classroom significantly lowered PM2.5 and black carbon, and schools using them district-wide had test scores 0.2 standard deviations higher than schools without, though ionizing units should be avoided because they generate ozone that can worsen asthma. [shard_03994_20629]
Modeling of a wildfire-smoke scenario found a portable air cleaner alone cuts indoor wildfire PM by about 45% in a home without central air, while pairing a higher-efficiency HVAC filter with a continuously running portable cleaner cuts it by roughly 62%, showing filtration and ventilation work best paired rather than treated as either-or choices. [shard_03994_20629]
A Washington study near an airport found portable HEPA units cut classroom ultrafine particle levels by about 70%, and a farmworker-community study found that giving families HEPA cleaners for children's bedrooms cut unplanned asthma medical visits by 72%, both in the kind of highway- and industry-adjacent, lower-income communities this district is asking about. [shard_04478_8349]
A Montana district's needs assessment found that outfitting nearly 700 unfiltered classrooms with portable HEPA units would cost roughly $107,000, versus a multi-year plan to add MERV-13-plus filtration to HVAC systems only as buildings are remodeled, illustrating why portable units are the realistic fix this year while HVAC becomes a capital-budget item. [shard_05805_11973]

Anti-idling rules deserve equal urgency because measured exposure inside diesel buses is exceptionally high.
NRDC and UC Berkeley researchers measured diesel exhaust inside school buses up to four times higher than in a car directly ahead of the bus, corresponding to a cancer risk 23 to 46 times the EPA's own significant-risk threshold. [shard_06042_74522]
Much of that pollution is "self-pollution" leaking back through doors, windows and cracks in the bus's own exhaust system, meaning closing windows does not fully protect riders, and idling buses at pickup lines concentrate emissions directly in the breathing zone of children queued to board. [shard_06104_10554]
Because pollution inhaled by the roughly 40 kids on one bus can be comparable to pollution inhaled by everyone else in a large city, CARB-recommended actions such as minimizing commute times, assigning the cleanest buses to the longest routes, and cutting idling and caravanning are unusually cost-effective. [shard_00357_50309]
Retrofitting existing diesel buses with particulate filters can cut particulate, hydrocarbon and carbon-monoxide emissions by 60 to 90%, and a documented boarding-exposure study supports a written no-idling policy at pickup and drop-off as a free action this year. [shard_04968_17585]

Electric buses are the right long-term goal but not a realistic this-year purchase for most districts.
A new electric bus costs roughly three to four times a diesel bus, about $225,000 to $375,000, even though it saves an estimated $2,000 to $4,400 per year in fuel and maintenance, with cost parity not expected until roughly the mid-to-late 2020s. [shard_05547_37834]
Smaller and rural districts may face extra delay, since one Alaska district's federal grant application was wait-listed even as demand tripled available funding, so districts should apply now for a multi-year rollout rather than expect near-term delivery. [shard_04468_6244]
EPA's Clean School Bus Program has intentionally directed two-thirds of funded electric buses to majority-communities-of-color districts and deployed twice as many buses in higher-pollution districts, so a district with highway-adjacent schools is a strong candidate for this funding even though delivery takes years. [shard_04338_49480]

HVAC filtration upgrades belong in the multi-year capital plan, but outside funding can accelerate them.
EPA used American Rescue Plan Act funds to help selected vulnerable communities retrofit school HVAC systems into cleaner-air and cooling-center hubs. [shard_06133_54048]
Colorado's EPA-funded program shows a realistic near-term bundle, combining portable air cleaners with indoor air quality monitors and smoke-readiness planning as one grant package instead of treating these as competing budget lines. [shard_03517_83875]

Monitoring is the cheapest layer and should underpin these decisions rather than compete with them for dollars.
A Fresno-area school near a highway installed a roughly $300 low-cost sensor because the nearest regulatory monitor, costing about $500,000 to install, was eight miles away and only approximated local conditions. [shard_01988_76094]
An Oregon district's six-school sensor network cost about $10,000 in hardware and directly informed decisions to move athletic practice indoors, showing monitoring can be deployed this year for a fraction of one HVAC retrofit. [shard_06060_54378]
Low-cost sensors correlate well with regulatory monitors but tend to overestimate PM2.5 by roughly a factor of two, so districts should apply EPA's correction guidance rather than read raw values at face value. [shard_01874_9042]

Weighed together, HEPA units and AQI rules offer the largest health benefit per dollar this year, monitors supply the data to trigger those rules consistently, anti-idling policies cost nothing while addressing the single highest measured child exposure, and HVAC retrofits and electric buses remain the most durable long-term fixes to pursue through grants and phased capital planning. [shard_05805_11973] [shard_05547_37834] [shard_06042_74522]
Because schools nearest highways and bus queues already carry the greatest baseline exposure and often serve more lower-income and Black, Indigenous and other students of color, equity argues for sequencing HEPA units, monitors and bus-idling rules at those campuses first, then directing HVAC and electric-bus grant applications to the same schools as funding arrives. [shard_04478_8349] [shard_04338_49480]

Low-cost sensors correlate well with regulatory monitors but tend to overestimate PM2.5 by roughly a factor of two, so districts should apply EPA's correction guidance rather than read raw values at face value.

Weighed together, HEPA units and AQI rules offer the largest health benefit per dollar this year, monitors supply data to trigger those rules consistently, anti-idling policies cost nothing while addressing the single highest measured child exposure, and HVAC retrofits and electric buses remain the most durable long-term fixes to pursue through grants and phased capital planning.

Because schools nearest highways and bus queues already carry the greatest baseline exposure and often serve more lower-income and Black, Indigenous and other students of color, equity argues for sequencing HEPA units, monitors and bus-idling rules there first, then directing HVAC and electric-bus grant applications to the same schools as funding arrives.
